title: Can PLTR Stock Live Up To Its Multiple?
detail:
Can PLTR Stock Live Up To Its Multiple?
Trefis Team
Fri, August 28, 2026 at 5:48 PM EDT 3 min read
PLTR
IBM
GOOG
AMZN
SNOW
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Image by Pexels from Pixabay

This is a hyper-growth chapter for Palantir Technologies. The company now provides a complete sovereign AI stack, with its AIP platform as the core engine for government and commercial clients.

This explosive U.S. growth is creating immense demand that strains the company's ability to scale. In response, management is now actively searching for technically competent partners to help meet this demand.

That's the story the market is currently paying 147.9x trailing earnings for. Has it taken the multiple too far, or is the growth implied by today's price reasonable? Let's unpack below.

Before we get into the math behind that valuation, PLTR's current numbers are worth keeping in mind as a reference point:

	

PLTR




Sector

	

Information Technology




Industry

	

Application Software


	


P/E Ratio

	

147.9




P/E Ratio 3Y Avg

	

238.5


	


LTM Revenue Growth

	

79%




3Y Avg Revenue Growth

	

46%


	


LTM Net Margin

	

49%




3Y Peak Net Margin

	

49%




3Y Avg Net Margin

	

23%

LTM refers to last twelve months.

What The Price Is Asking For

To defend PLTR's $446.2B market cap over the next 7 years, three things have to play out. The multiple settles from today's 147.9x toward 28.8x, the multiple a mature, scaled software franchise typically settles into. Margins land near 35%, set near the midpoint of the company's own margin cycle, since its peak clears mature peers but its through-cycle average sits well below that peak. And revenue compounds from $6.2B today to $44.3B at maturity, supporting $15.5B of annual net income. That last line works out to a required revenue CAGR of 33%, below the 79% the business is currently running.

Is This Realistic?

Growth is being driven by accelerating adoption in the U.S. commercial segment. Existing customers are also expanding their use from the Foundry platform to the full Ontology and AI stack. The company is also entering the market for fine-tuning models, expanding its role beyond orchestration.

The company's current growth and margins are at a cyclical peak, far above its historical average. Management has already signaled a significant expense ramp for the coming quarter due to new hiring. This spending, combined with a heavy reliance on the booming U.S. market, creates risk of margin reversion if growth moderates.

Today's price needs less growth than the business is currently delivering. But that current pace is a cyclical peak, not a sustainable rate. In a normal year, the bar is meaningfully higher.

The challenge is finding enough competent partners to scale its U.S. boom before cyclical pressures cause margins to revert.

title: Dell Stock Widens Your Portfolio Instead Of Steadying It
detail:
Dell Stock Widens Your Portfolio Instead Of Steadying It
Trefis Team
Fri, August 28, 2026 at 5:05 PM EDT 3 min read
DELL
^GSPC
HPQ
IBM
AAPL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Its five-year correlation to the broad market leaves real room for behavior of its own, but the swing that comes with it is far wider than the index's.

Dell Technologies (DELL) stock has climbed 8.6% over the last five trading days while the S&P 500 added 1.2%, and the urge to chase a run like that is real. That five-day stretch is not the question this piece answers. The question is how much of DELL's return is its own story rather than the index you already own, and what holding it does to your swings.

What A 0.49 Correlation Actually Means

Over the past five years, DELL's daily moves have tracked the S&P 500 at a correlation of 0.49. A reading of 1.0 would be perfect lockstep and 0 would mean the two are unrelated, so the stock shares part of the market's direction while keeping substantial behavior of its own. Gold's correlation to DELL over the same five years is 0.1, so 0.49 is a real but partial tie to the index rather than a clean break from it. DELL's annualized return over those five years was 60.5%, against 12.8% for the index. It did so at 52.7% annualized volatility, roughly three times the index's 17.2%.

It Went The Market's Way, Then Went Much Further

The one-year capture readings and the five-year correlation measure different things. Correlation asks whether two things move in the same direction. Capture asks how far. On days the S&P 500 rose over the past year, DELL captured about 291% of the gain; on days it fell, DELL absorbed about 179% of the loss. It moves with the market often, then moves much further on its own account.

Memory Supply, Not The Index, Gates What Dell Ships

What carries Dell that much further than the index sits inside the operation. Dell booked $43.8 billion of revenue in fiscal Q1 2027, up 88%, with ISG revenue up 181% and AI servers alone up nearly 9x year over year to $16.1 billion, and left that quarter with a record $51.3 billion AI backlog, an order book larger than the whole quarter's revenue.

Management says demand is running ahead of supply and names memory as the primary constraint, with DRAM and NAND the tight commodities. What Dell ships therefore turns on component allocation and component prices, which the S&P 500 does not set. Dell also runs through a thin P&L: an 8.1% operating margin against an S&P 500 median of 18.5%, a 7.0% free-cash-flow margin against 14.5%, so input costs land on profit with force. Profitability that thin sits at the opposite end from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, which holds quality businesses with strong margins and cash generation.

title: How Wide Is The Risk Band On IBM Stock?
detail:
How Wide Is The Risk Band On IBM Stock?
Trefis Team
Fri, August 28, 2026 at 1:49 PM EDT 3 min read
IBM
ACN
MSFT
AMZN
ORCL-PD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

The one-year range the options market puts around this stock runs past both ends of what it has actually traded, and for this stock that width is an ordinary reading rather than an alarm.

International Business Machines (IBM) trades at about $239, and its option chain has already drawn the box its shareholders are standing in. Over roughly the year ahead the market prices a two-in-three chance the stock finishes between $158 and $360. That is a $202 spread on a $239 stock.

The Priced Floor Sits Under The Fifty-Two Week Low

The band runs from $158 to $360, both ends outside the $204 to $327 range the stock has actually traded over the past 52 weeks. In a holder's money, the floor is $78.79 a share below today's price, about a third of the position, and the ceiling is $121 above it. That is not a forecast, and not the whole risk: roughly a one-in-six chance sits beyond each end. That $79 is the size of fall a holder has to be able to sit through.

Enterprise License Agreements Are Why Transaction Processing Revenue Arrives In Lumps

In the second quarter of 2026, large deals numbering in the low tens missed the timelines management had expected, and transaction processing revenue fell 9% even as data revenue grew 18%, both at constant currency, with clients redirecting near-term CapEx budgets toward third-party servers, storage, and memory ahead of expected industry price increases. Because those transaction processing deals are structured as large enterprise license agreements signed alongside mainframe deployments, competing against that urgent hardware spend meant a few weeks of client hesitation landed as a whole quarter. Management now guides full-year 2026 revenue growth to 4% to 5%, calling the low end its base case, and reads the shortfall as demand deferred rather than destroyed, with about a third of the slipped deals closed within three weeks. Revenue that arrives in lumps that large carries a wide set of outcomes around it.

Options Are Pricing A Calmer Year Than The One Just Delivered

The past twelve months delivered a 1.0% return against 20.5% for the S&P 500, on realized volatility of 48.6%: plenty of movement, nothing to show for it. The implied volatility on those year-out options is 39.9%, below what the stock has actually delivered, which does not happen often: the market is looking for the action to settle, not intensify. Measured against its own history rather than against realized movement, a broader reading of IBM implied volatility sits at the 49th percentile of its own trailing one-year range, squarely mid-scale for this stock. A $200 spread is what an ordinary year looks like here. Nor is the operation coming apart: revenue is $69.1 billion over the trailing twelve months, up 7.9% as reported, before the guided step down to 4% to 5% at constant currency (roughly 2.5% to 3.5% as reported), with an operating margin of 18.4% against a 16.6% three-year average. Growth and margin of that shape are what the Trefis High Quality Portfolio favors in its holdings.

title: The Smaller Customers Accenture's Stock Now Needs
detail:
The Smaller Customers Accenture's Stock Now Needs
Trefis Team

ACN
CTSH
IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

Accenture's consulting weakness sits in large-enterprise discretionary budgets, and its clearest upside case is a mid-market push that does not need them to thaw.

Accenture (ACN) stock is down about 24% over the past year and trades roughly 34% below its 52-week high, even after gaining 6.3% over the trailing three months, leaving a market capitalization of about $114.7 billion. The business behind it is not shrinking, and its soft spot is narrower than that decline suggests. The strongest upside case does not depend on large-enterprise budgets reopening at all.

The Consulting Weakness Sits In Discretionary Work

In fiscal Q3 2026, consulting revenue grew 1% in local currency against 5% for managed services, and management attributes a roughly $100 million revenue shortfall against its expectations to the Middle East conflict, all of it consulting work. That is the discretionary end of the business, the smaller and faster-cycling work large enterprises buy, and the first spending they stop. Management calls it an industry problem several years old, not a single noisy quarter. In sales, management put the conflict's impact at roughly $400 million in the Middle East.

Accenture Edge Aims At A Customer It Never Made A Focus

The response is not to wait. In late June the company launched Accenture Edge, a business for companies with $300 million to $3 billion of revenue, a pool management sizes at $240 billion, growing at a high-single-digit rate. Management's stated purpose is to structurally offset the large-enterprise discretionary weakness.

Mid-market clients do not need the account coverage model Accenture runs for large enterprises, the route in is ecosystem-led, and Avanade, its joint venture, already serves mid-market clients. In the past week the company has agreed to acquire McCoy, a Dutch SAP transformation partner for mid-market companies, and Comware, a Tokyo-based provider of end-to-end technology services, with the latter deal framed as strengthening Accenture Edge.

Set that $240 billion addressable market against $73.1 billion of trailing revenue and the honest read is not that one launch transforms a company this size. It is that Accenture is opening, from a position of operating strength, a market that management concedes has never been a focus. Reported revenue growth over the trailing twelve months, at 6.7%, is ahead of the company's 4.8% three-year pace. Net margin at 10.7% runs just below its 11.0% three-year average; the trailing operating margin of 15.8% sits at its own three-year peak. Growing revenue while the operating margin sits at a peak is the property the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for in its holdings.

detail:
Is Oracle Stock Getting Too Cheap To Ignore After A 53% Drop?

IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Image from Pixabay

For Oracle stock, the upside now depends less on the size of the order book than on the pace at which the company can energize what it has already sold.

Oracle (ORCL) has spent the past year getting cheaper while its order book got bigger. The stock is down about 34% over the trailing twelve months and sits roughly 53% below its high of the past year, at a market value of about $436.8 billion, even as contracted future work reached $638 billion.

Just 12% Of The Backlog Is Expected To Reach Revenue Inside A Year

Remaining performance obligations finished fiscal 2026 at $638 billion, up from $553 billion at the end of fiscal Q3 2026. Management expects 12% of that to convert within twelve months, roughly $77 billion, against $67.4 billion of revenue over the trailing twelve months, and sees that share accelerating over the coming quarters. Oracle earns that trailing-twelve-month revenue at an operating margin of 33.3%, its own three-year peak, so what comes next starts from strength rather than repair. Demand is not the constraint; a contract pays only once a data hall is energized and handed to the customer.

Oracle Guides One Quarter To Nearly Match What Fiscal 2026 Delivered In Four

Oracle handed customers more than 1.2 gigawatts across fiscal 2026, and more than 400 megawatts of that landed in fiscal Q3 2026. Management said in June that fiscal Q1 2027 delivery was approaching a gigawatt on its own, close to the previous four quarters combined. At Abilene, Texas, the company had delivered 42% of total capacity as of June, with a further 35% then due inside ninety days. In Shackelford County, Texas, first power came online ahead of schedule. Owning the shares is primarily dependent on one company's build-out arriving on time, a different proposition from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, whose returns do not rest on the handful of largest technology names.

The Customers Are Pre-Funding Part Of The Build

What matters is the shape of the $67 billion of AI infrastructure contracts signed in fiscal Q4 2026: the majority were either bring your own hardware or prepaid, taking Oracle's cumulative pool of such contracts to $75 billion, which management says carries no margin degradation against its other contracts. The customers most eager for capacity help fund the plant that serves them, lowering the cash Oracle itself must raise. Fiscal 2027 still calls for about $70 billion of net cash capital spending, a figure already net of $20 billion to $25 billion of customer prepayments and timing. Funding it takes around $40 billion of debt and equity, including a $20 billion at-the-market issuance already announced.

Sound complicated? With StockStory, it doesn't have to be. Our job is to find you high-quality companies that can win regardless of the conditions. Keeping that in mind, here is one industry titan whose competitive advantages create flywheel effects and two that could be stalling.

Two Mega-Cap Stocks to Sell:

With a corporate history spanning over a century and once known for its iconic mainframe computers, IBM (NYSE:IBM) provides hybrid cloud computing platforms, AI solutions, consulting services, and enterprise infrastructure to help businesses modernize their operations.

Why Is IBM Not Exciting?

Why Will MU Beat the Market?

Annual revenue growth of 106% over the last two years was superb and indicates its market share increased during this cycle

Incremental sales significantly boosted profitability as its annual earnings per share growth of 57.1% over the last five years outstripped its revenue performance

title: Can High Gate Fidelity Justify Buying Rigetti Stock Today?
detail:
Can High Gate Fidelity Justify Buying Rigetti Stock Today?
Trefis Team

RGTI
^GSPC
QUBT
IBM
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by StockSnap on Pixabay

Buying the stock today means paying for an engineering roadmap that runs years out, not for the hardware revenue the company books now.

Rigetti Computing (RGTI), a Nasdaq-listed maker of superconducting quantum computers, trades about 71% below its 52-week high, and it has gained 24.4% over the past month. What the price buys is an engineering roadmap, and how credible that roadmap looks is the whole of the case.

What 410 Times Sales Is Attached To

Even after a 39.2% fall over the past three months, against a 2.2% gain for the S&P 500, the stock trades at a price-to-sales ratio of 410.2 versus 3.3 for the index. That multiple sits on $13.4 million of revenue over the trailing twelve months, a base small enough that the ratio prices the future, not the present. Rigetti sells cloud access to its Cepheus-1-108Q system and on-premises Novera QPU hardware to national labs and universities.

The Revenue Line Is A Delivery Calendar

Second-quarter 2026 revenue reached $5.1 million from $1.8 million a year earlier, an increase the company attributes to on-premises Novera QPU sales. The $8.4 million C-DAC order for a 108-qubit system in India, which the company expects to recognize in the fourth quarter of 2026, is on its own close to two-thirds of the entire trailing-twelve-month revenue base. By the company's own account revenue is shaped by the timing of system deliveries and government-funded projects.

Coherence Time, Not Qubit Count, Is The Constraint

Cepheus-1-108Q is assembled from 12 interconnected 9-qubit chiplets, and management says only three gate-based machines anywhere run above 100 qubits: this one, IBM's and Google's. Qubit count, though, is not where the difficulty sits. Coherence times of 25 to 30 microseconds are, on the company's own account, the primary limit on two-qubit gate fidelity, and the chip design and materials work meant to double or triple them is expected to play out over several years. That timetable is the real clock on the 99.9% two-qubit fidelity that Rigetti's roughly three-year, 1,000-qubit roadmap objective calls for.

What Pays For The Wait

The second quarter of 2026 produced a $28.1 million operating loss, wider than the $19.9 million a year earlier, as spending went into fabrication and refrigeration capacity. Funding that loss is $541.3 million of cash, equivalents and available-for-sale investments at the end of June 2026, down from $569 million three months earlier, and no debt at all. The Trefis High Quality Portfolio holds businesses with defensible balance sheets.

The trio below pulls together a full-year cash-flow calendar using three of the sturdiest dividend payers in the S&P 500, one of which has now paid a dividend every year since 1916.

jittawit21 / Shutterstock.com
Cisco Systems: The January, April, July, October Anchor

Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) writes checks in January, April, July, and October, making it the natural first leg of this 12-month bundle. The quarterly payout is $0.42 per share, with an annualized forward dividend of $1.68 and a yield of 1.49% at a share price of $112.

In terms of recent results, Cisco generated $5.4 billion of operating cash flow in Q4 alone and closed FY26 with $15.9 billion in cash and investments. Management returned $12.7 billion to shareholders in fiscal 2026, split between $6.6 billion in cash dividends and $6.1 billion of share repurchases, which CEO Chuck Robbins pegged at 99% of free cash flow. The track record: Cisco "increased our dividend for the 15th consecutive year in FY26."

The bull case for income investors is that the payout is being financed by an AI networking upcycle rather than a slow-growth cash cow. FY26 revenue hit $63.3 billion, up 12%, and FY27 guidance calls for revenue of $72.2 billion to $73.4 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $5.05 to $5.11. That gives the $1.68 annualized dividend enormous coverage.
